item.title: US Senate cannot "run out the clock" on Hegseth impeachment, warns Republican Thomas Massie
item.description: Outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie has moved to impeach US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran, introducing eight articles of impeachment that accuse him of illegally waging ...
item.content:encoded:
US Senate cannot "run out the clock" on Hegseth impeachment, warns Republican Thomas Massie  Outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie introduced articles of impeachment against US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth over the Iran war. Massie and Indian-American Congressman Ro Khanna stressed that the Senate cannot run out the clock, while President Trump stood by Hegseth. ANI | Updated: 10-11-2026 09:56 IST | Created: 10-11-2026 09:56 IST

Outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie (left) and US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie has moved to impeach US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran, introducing eight articles of impeachment that accuse him of illegally waging war without congressional authorisation and abusing his powers as Pentagon chief. Addressing the developments during an appearance on CNN's The Source alongside Indian-American Congressman Ro Khanna, Massie emphasised that the Senate cannot evade impeachment proceedings by delaying action until the next legislative session. Discussing the articles of impeachment filed against Hegseth, Massie explained the procedural distinction governing congressional resolutions, stating, "If the Speaker and the Senate Majority Leader are somehow able to push this into the next Congress, for every other bill and resolution, they expire at the end of this Congress. But for impeachments, they go into the next Congress. And so the Senate can't run out the clock on this one." Weighing in on the discussion during the broadcast, Ro Khanna underscored Massie's principled stance on Capitol Hill, pointing out the personal and professional toll such positions often exact by noting, "Thomas literally gave up his career because he stood up on the war on Iran and on the Epstein files." Hegseth had "knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders" by waging war without congressional approval, Massie, a critic of Donald Trump who lost his primary to a candidate backed by the President, stated on the House floor. The articles cite violations of the 1973 War Powers Resolution, alongside misconduct involving civilian casualties and operations in Yemen and Venezuela. Hegseth, a former Fox News weekend host and one of Trump's handpicked appointments in his second term as US President, took charge of the Department of War despite lacking administrative experience commensurate with the post. Despite controversies surrounding his tenure as Secretary of War, Trump has maintained his support for Hegseth and repeatedly dismissed suggestions of dismissing him. While bipartisan backing for impeachment has grown, one of Trump's staunch allies in Congress, House Speaker Mike Johnson, has blocked previous initiatives, contending that impeaching a Cabinet secretary amid active hostilities abroad projects a "terrible look" to both allies and adversaries. When Massie initially sought to present the resolution as a privileged motion in September, Johnson countered by abruptly adjourning the House and dismissing lawmakers nearly seven weeks early for the midterms, successfully deferring the vote beyond Election Day. Nevertheless, the midterm outcome fell short of Republican expectations, with Democrats poised to seize control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives by January 2027, heightening Hegseth's vulnerability. Incoming Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries, projected to assume the speakership in January, stated on Sunday that he was a "hard yes" on impeachment, telling ABC News, "The so-called Secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran." "Pete Hegseth has got to go," Jeffries added. Trump reaffirmed his backing for Hegseth on Monday, asserting that he had performed a "good job" and "won" conflicts in Venezuela and Iran, pointing to the rapid raid that captured Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in January, alongside the prolonged eight-month conflict with Tehran. In response to queries regarding a potential impeachment of Hegseth, Trump told reporters, "Yeah, I'll stand by him." Trump additionally dismissed Massie as a "stone cold loser" over the impeachment push. (ANI)

item.title: Nvidia, CEO Jensen Huang sued by shareholders over alleged concealment of suspected Chinese spy links
item.description: Nvidia and its Chief Executive Jensen Huang have been sued in a proposed class-action lawsuit accusing them of misleading shareholders by concealing Huang's alleged ties to a woman suspected of ...
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia, CEO Jensen Huang sued by shareholders over alleged concealment of suspected Chinese spy links Nvidia and its Chief Executive Jensen Huang have been sued in a proposed class-action lawsuit accusing them of misleading shareholders by concealing Huang's alleged ties to a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, adding to growing scrutiny over the chipmaker's business and national security exposure, according to a Reuters report. ANI | Updated: 10-11-2026 09:55 IST | Created: 10-11-2026 09:55 IST

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (Photo/Nvidia). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Nvidia and its Chief Executive Jensen Huang have been sued in a proposed class-action lawsuit accusing them of misleading shareholders by concealing Huang's alleged ties to a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, adding to growing scrutiny over the chipmaker's business and national security exposure, according to a Reuters report. The complaint, filed on Monday in a federal court in San Jose, California, alleges that Nvidia and Huang failed to disclose the relationship and the national security concerns it raised, which the shareholders claim threatened the company's reputation and business prospects. The lawsuit concerns Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed. The New York Times reported last month that US authorities had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia's board announced an investigation into the matter on Sunday, with independent directors engaging external legal counsel to examine the circumstances surrounding the relationship. The company has maintained that there is no evidence that national security or proprietary corporate information was compromised, according to earlier reports. The proposed class-action lawsuit, filed by shareholders led by Mark Kistenmacher, alleges that Nvidia and Huang failed to disclose the relationship and the national security concerns surrounding it. The shareholders are seeking unspecified damages, Reuters reported. Huang had earlier addressed the personal matter in a communication to employees, acknowledging his infidelity. "I was unfaithful to my wife," he said. The controversy has also drawn attention from US lawmakers over the distribution of advanced artificial intelligence chips and the possibility of restricted technology reaching China through third countries. Democratic members of the House Foreign Affairs Committee have sought answers from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the administration's export policies, while Republican lawmakers have also sought a closed-door discussion with Huang. Nvidia shares closed 4.3 per cent lower on Monday, wiping out approximately USD 190 billion from the company's market capitalisation, Reuters reported. The lawsuit was filed five minutes after the US stock market closed. The legal proceedings and ongoing board investigation could keep attention on Nvidia's disclosure practices and the scrutiny surrounding its technology exports as the company faces questions over the alleged relationship and its potential implications. (ANI)

item.title: US-Israel security pact set to halve direct military aid post-2028 under evolving five-year framework: Report
item.description: New details reveal US military aid to Israel will not end immediately, but will instead be halved to a five-year package after 2028. Negotiators aim to finalise the memorandum of understanding before ...
item.content:encoded:
US-Israel security pact set to halve direct military aid post-2028 under evolving five-year framework: Report  New details reveal US military aid to Israel will not end immediately, but will instead be halved to a five-year package after 2028. Negotiators aim to finalise the memorandum of understanding before January, navigating domestic political hurdles and potential congressional appropriations challenges. ANI | Updated: 09-11-2026 14:57 IST | Created: 09-11-2026 14:57 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

American military assistance to Israel will not terminate immediately under a forthcoming security memorandum of understanding, with new details uncovered by Ynetnews indicating that direct aid will instead be reduced by roughly half by restricting its duration to a five-year window following 2028 rather than the traditional decade-long span. These revelations surface approximately a week after US President Donald Trump unexpectedly stated that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed to halt American military aid by the close of the year, leaving Israeli negotiating teams bewildered by the pronouncement, as reported by Ynetnews. A senior Israeli official assessed that Trump's declaration was driven primarily by domestic political calculations to assist Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan against Democratic challenger Abdul El-Sayed, though the strategy ultimately proved unsuccessful as El-Sayed secured victory, becoming the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, according to Ynetnews. During a Fox News appearance on Election Day, Trump stated, "We were giving them $4 billion. We are, but it gets cut off at the end of the year." He additionally noted that Netanyahu had previously raised the concept of phasing out assistance on the grounds that Israel had evolved into a prosperous nation no longer requiring such backing. Nevertheless, the evolving framework does not contemplate an immediate stoppage, with current assistance remaining fully active through 2028 under the prevailing model that grants USD 3.3 billion yearly in Foreign Military Financing alongside USD 500 million for joint defence research, Ynetnews noted. Under the revised terms under discussion by teams representing US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Israel's Defence Ministry, annual funding levels would remain comparable for a shortened five-year period totalling roughly USD 16.5 billion before direct military provisions cease. Meanwhile, American allocations dedicated to collaborative air and missile defence advancement are anticipated to climb from the present USD 500 million annually to an amount yet to be finalised. Furthermore, a senior Israeli official familiar with the diplomatic exchanges observed that numerous members of Congress resist lowering assistance due to domestic economic factors, given that the vast majority of funds flow directly back into American manufacturing plants and local state economies, as detailed by Ynetnews. "We are moving here from a model of aid to a model of partnership," the senior Israeli official stated, adding, "It is important to remember that most of the security assistance remains in America and contributes to the American economy. Cutting it would also hurt American industries and require adjustments." While negotiators aim to conclude the pact prior to the new Congress convening in January, Israeli planners remain wary regarding annual congressional appropriation hurdles and potential political friction. Officials have acknowledged that future government compositions and leadership figures will heavily influence legislative backing in Washington, Ynetnews reported. (ANI)
